questions.question_html: $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in methyl chloride compared to $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene is

questions.explanation_text: The $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in methyl chloride is compared with the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene. In methyl chloride, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{Cl}$ , carbon is $sp^{3}$ hybridised and the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond is a normal single bond. In chlorobenzene, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$ , the chlorine atom is attached to an $sp^{2}$ hybridised carbon of the benzene ring. Also, due to resonance, the lone pair of chlorine overlaps with the benzene ring. This gives the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond some partial double bond character. Because of this partial double bond character, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene is shorter and stronger than in methyl chloride. So, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in methyl chloride is: $\text{longer and weaker}$ Correct option: D.
questions.explanation_html:
The $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in methyl chloride is compared with the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene.

In methyl chloride, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{Cl}$ , carbon is $sp^{3}$ hybridised and the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond is a normal single bond.

In chlorobenzene, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$ , the chlorine atom is attached to an $sp^{2}$ hybridised carbon of the benzene ring. Also, due to resonance, the lone pair of chlorine overlaps with the benzene ring. This gives the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond some partial double bond character.

Because of this partial double bond character, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene is shorter and stronger than in methyl chloride.

So, the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond in methyl chloride is:

$\text{longer and weaker}$

Correct option: D.

questions.question_html: In $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ reaction, the alkyl halide that on hydrolysis produces racemic mixture is

options.label: A
options.html: Tertiary butyl bromide

options.label: B
options.html: 2-bromobutane

options.label: C
options.html: Isopropyl bromide

options.label: D
options.html: Methyl bromide

questions.explanation_text: The correct option is B. 2-bromobutane . In an $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ reaction, the alkyl halide first forms a carbocation. This carbocation is planar , so the nucleophile can attack from either side with almost equal chance. For 2-bromobutane , $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CHBr}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$ the carbon bearing bromine is a chiral carbon. During hydrolysis, bromide ion leaves and forms a planar carbocation: $\text{CH}_{3}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$ Water can attack this carbocation from both sides, producing both enantiomers of butan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$ So a racemic mixture is formed. Tertiary butyl bromide also undergoes $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ , but the product tert-butyl alcohol is not chiral, so it does not give a racemic mixture. Hence, the answer is: $\text{Option B: 2-bromobutane}$
questions.explanation_html:
The correct option is B. 2-bromobutane.

In an $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ reaction, the alkyl halide first forms a carbocation. This carbocation is planar, so the nucleophile can attack from either side with almost equal chance.

For 2-bromobutane,

$\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CHBr}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$

the carbon bearing bromine is a chiral carbon. During hydrolysis, bromide ion leaves and forms a planar carbocation:

$\text{CH}_{3}-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$

Water can attack this carbocation from both sides, producing both enantiomers of butan-2-ol:

$\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$

So a racemic mixture is formed.

Tertiary butyl bromide also undergoes $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ , but the product tert-butyl alcohol is not chiral, so it does not give a racemic mixture.

Hence, the answer is:

$\text{Option B: 2-bromobutane}$

questions.question_html: The compound from which chlorobenzene cannot be prepared easily is

options.label: A
options.html: Aniline

options.label: B
options.html: Benzene

options.label: C
options.html: Phenol

options.label: D
options.html: Benzene diazonium chloride

questions.explanation_text: Chlorobenzene cannot be prepared easily from phenol . In phenol, the $-OH$ group is directly attached to the benzene ring. The carbon-oxygen bond in phenol has partial double bond character due to resonance, so it is not easily broken. Because of this, replacing $-OH$ by $-Cl$ is difficult. The other options can give chlorobenzene quite easily: From benzene: $C_{6}H_{6}+Cl_{2}\overset{FeCl_{3}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}Cl+HCl$ From aniline, first diazotisation is done, then Sandmeyer reaction: $C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2}\bar{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}$ $C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}\overset{CuCl/HCl}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}Cl+N_{2}$ From benzene diazonium chloride: $C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}\overset{CuCl/HCl}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}Cl+N_{2}$ So the correct option is: $\text{Option C: Phenol}$
questions.explanation_html:
Chlorobenzene cannot be prepared easily from phenol.

In phenol, the $-OH$ group is directly attached to the benzene ring. The carbon-oxygen bond in phenol has partial double bond character due to resonance, so it is not easily broken. Because of this, replacing $-OH$ by $-Cl$ is difficult.

The other options can give chlorobenzene quite easily:

From benzene:

$C_{6}H_{6}+Cl_{2}\overset{FeCl_{3}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}Cl+HCl$

From aniline, first diazotisation is done, then Sandmeyer reaction:

$C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2}\bar{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}$

$C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}\overset{CuCl/HCl}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}Cl+N_{2}$

From benzene diazonium chloride:

$C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}\overset{CuCl/HCl}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C_{6}H_{5}Cl+N_{2}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option C: Phenol}$

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true is case of alkyl halides?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements is true is case of alkyl halides?

options.label: A
options.html: They are polar in nature

options.label: B
options.html: They can form hydrogen bonds

options.label: C
options.text: They are highly soluble in water
options.html: They are highly soluble in water

options.label: D
options.html: They undergo addition reactions

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze each option: $\text{Option A: They are polar in nature}$ Alkyl halides have a $\text{C–X}$ bond (where X is a halogen such as Cl, Br, or I). The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, which creates a dipole in the bond. Even though the overall molecular polarity can depend on the molecular structure, the presence of the $\text{C–X}$ bond makes them polar in nature. Therefore, Option A is true. $\text{Option B: They can form hydrogen bonds}$ For a molecule to form hydrogen bonds, it must have a hydrogen atom attached to a highly electronegative atom like $\text{O}$ , $\text{N}$ , or $\text{F}$ . In alkyl halides, the hydrogens are bonded to carbon, not to the halogen. Hence, they do not participate in hydrogen bonding. $\text{Option C: They are highly soluble in water}$ While the $\text{C–X}$ bond is polar, alkyl halides have relatively large nonpolar hydrocarbon parts. This makes them largely insoluble in water since water is a highly polar solvent and mixes well only with similarly polar substances. $\text{Option D: They undergo addition reactions}$ Addition reactions typically occur with unsaturated compounds (such as alkenes or alkynes). Alkyl halides are saturated compounds (only $\sigma$ bonds) and do not undergo addition reactions under normal conditions. Given the explanations, the correct statement is: $\text{Option A: They are polar in nature}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let's analyze each option:

$\text{Option A: They are polar in nature}$

Alkyl halides have a $\text{C–X}$ bond (where X is a halogen such as Cl, Br, or I).

The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, which creates a dipole in the bond.

Even though the overall molecular polarity can depend on the molecular structure, the presence of the $\text{C–X}$ bond makes them polar in nature.

Therefore, Option A is true.

$\text{Option B: They can form hydrogen bonds}$

For a molecule to form hydrogen bonds, it must have a hydrogen atom attached to a highly electronegative atom like $\text{O}$ , $\text{N}$ , or $\text{F}$ .

In alkyl halides, the hydrogens are bonded to carbon, not to the halogen.

Hence, they do not participate in hydrogen bonding.

$\text{Option C: They are highly soluble in water}$

While the $\text{C–X}$ bond is polar, alkyl halides have relatively large nonpolar hydrocarbon parts.

This makes them largely insoluble in water since water is a highly polar solvent and mixes well only with similarly polar substances.

$\text{Option D: They undergo addition reactions}$

Addition reactions typically occur with unsaturated compounds (such as alkenes or alkynes).

Alkyl halides are saturated compounds (only $\sigma$ bonds) and do not undergo addition reactions under normal conditions.

Given the explanations, the correct statement is:

$\text{Option A: They are polar in nature}$

questions.question_text: Tertiary alkyl halide is practically inert to substitution by $S_{N}2$ mechanism because of
questions.question_html: Tertiary alkyl halide is practically inert to substitution by $S_{N}2$ mechanism because of

options.label: A
options.html: insolubility

options.label: B
options.html: instability

options.label: C
options.html: inductive effect

options.label: D
options.html: steric hindrance

questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option D: steric hindrance. Here's why: In an $S_{N}2$ reaction, the nucleophile must approach the electrophilic carbon from behind (the side opposite the leaving group) to displace it. Tertiary alkyl halides have three bulky alkyl groups around the reactive carbon. These bulky groups create steric hindrance, which physically blocks the nucleophile from accessing the carbon center. Because the nucleophile cannot effectively approach the electrophilic center, the $S_{N}2$ reaction is significantly slowed down or doesn’t occur at all. Thus, tertiary alkyl halides are practically inert to substitution by the $S_{N}2$ mechanism due to steric hindrance.
questions.explanation_html:
The correct answer is Option D: steric hindrance.

Here's why:

In an $S_{N}2$ reaction, the nucleophile must approach the electrophilic carbon from behind (the side opposite the leaving group) to displace it.

Because the nucleophile cannot effectively approach the electrophilic center, the $S_{N}2$ reaction is significantly slowed down or doesn’t occur at all.

Thus, tertiary alkyl halides are practically inert to substitution by the $S_{N}2$ mechanism due to steric hindrance.
